title: When things fail
summary: Panics for bugs, Result for the failures you can plan for, and the ? operator.

blocks.html: Two different things can go wrong in a program. There are bugs: our own code is wrong, or a promise we made to ourselves has been broken. And there are legitimate failures: the user typed letters into a field that wants a number, the file we expected is not on disk. Rust gives each one its own tool, and mixing them up is the fastest way to write a program nobody can debug.

blocks.title: panic.rs

blocks.html:
A panic! is Rust giving up on this program. The message goes to standard error, not standard output, and the process exits with a nonzero code:

thread 'main' (4276) panicked at main.rs:3:5:
no config file found
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

The number in parentheses is the thread id and changes on every run; the rest is fixed. A backtrace is the chain of calls that led here — the note tells you how to ask for one. There is no recovering from this point in the program.

blocks.title: unwrap and expect

blocks.html:
unwrap() and expect(msg) say the same thing — give me the value or panic — and differ only in the message. unwrap panics with the standard text, called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }; expect panics with your sentence, and six months from now that sentence is the only clue you get. Use expect.

A panic ends the program, which is a rude answer to bad input. For failures we can plan for, Rust makes the failure a value: parse returns Result<i32, ParseIntError>, and a Result is either Ok(value) or Err(error). It is an enum, so match reads it.

blocks.title: matching a Result
blocks.output:
42 is the number 42
forty-two is not a number: invalid digit found in string

blocks.title: Result is a shape with two boxes
blocks.ascii:
Result<T, E>
+----------------------+   +----------------------+
| Ok(value)            |   | Err(error)           |
| the number we wanted |   | why it did not work  |
+----------------------+   +----------------------+

never both. A match opens one box or the other.

blocks.html: Writing a match at every step gets old fast. The ? operator does it for you: on an Ok it unwraps the value and carries on; on an Err it returns that error from the function immediately. The catch is that the function using ? must itself return a Result — there has to be somewhere for the error to go.

blocks.title: the ? operator

blocks.html:
fn main() may return a Result, which is why ? is legal there. () is the success value — main has nothing to hand back — and Box<dyn std::error::Error> means any error type at all. dyn is a trait object; lesson 13 is where traits get their turn. Read it for now as "whatever went wrong": a failed ? in main prints Error: ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit } and exits nonzero.

Three helpers never panic. unwrap_or(fallback) gives the value or a default. unwrap_or_else(closure) calls the closure only when there was an error, so the fallback can log the reason. ok() throws the error away and leaves an Option<T> — Some(value) or None — for when you only care whether a value came out.

blocks.title: unwrapping without panicking
blocks.output:
falling back because invalid digit found in string
42 0 -1 Some(42) None

blocks.html: Rule of thumb. Use Result for anything a caller might handle differently: bad input, a missing file, a network timeout. Use panic!, unwrap, and expect when the alternative is a program in an impossible state — an index you just checked, a string your own code wrote. A library that panics on bad input takes that choice away from its caller.

quiz.q: A user types seven into a field that should hold a number. What should your function do?
options: Return a Result so the caller can decide what to show
Return the number 0 and carry on
quiz.why: Bad input is a failure we can plan for, so it becomes an Err value. A panic ends the whole program and gives the caller no say; returning 0 quietly turns a typo into wrong data.

quiz.q: A function returns Result. What does ? do when it meets an Err?
options: It panics with the error message
It returns that error from the function immediately
quiz.why: ? is a match in one character: on Ok it unwraps the value, on Err it returns the error to the caller, which is why the function must return a Result.

quiz.q: Which of these panics with a message you wrote yourself?
quiz.why: expect takes your text and includes it in the panic. unwrap panics with the standard message, and unwrap_or never panics at all.

exercise.brief: Fill in parse_all: parse both strings, add them, and return the sum wrapped in Ok. Use ? so a bad number comes back as Err.
exercise.hint: parse needs to know the type it is producing, so write let x: i32 = a.parse()?; and the same for b. Then Ok(x + y). The ? works because this function already returns a Result.
